title: Jensen Huang didn’t believe in succession plans. Your startup shouldn’t make the same mistake | BetaKit
html:
Erin Bury is the co-founder and CEO of online estate planning company Willful.


In a March 2026 podcast interview, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that he doesn’t believe in succession planning and that he could be CEO “until the last day of my life.” Seven months later, he resigned amid a scandal over his multiple alleged affairs, and his multi-billion-dollar company was left without a clear successor. 

Beyond the affair, this was Huang’s biggest mistake: believing that because he didn’t plan to exit the business, he didn’t need to plan for a successor or set the business up to run smoothly without him.

“Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence.”

Every founder needs a succession plan, both for themselves and their key people, regardless of whether they plan to sell the business or not. Despite the importance, the CFIB reported in October that only six percent of Canadian small business owners have a formal written succession plan. We can’t predict the future; succession planning covers both planned absences, including parental leaves and sabbaticals, and unplanned absences due to illness, death, family caregiving requirements, or, like Huang, a public scandal.

If you’re a founder who falls into the 94 percent of business owners who don’t have a formal succession plan, here are the key steps to put in place.

Create a written succession plan for key leaders

Many business owners have playbooks for what to do if a crisis happens. Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence. At Willful, we work with the value creation firm Horizon; they had us go through the exercise of creating a formal succession plan for my husband and me, as well as our key leaders. It asked questions I hadn’t thought about, like:

  • Who would take over this person’s responsibilities if they were unexpectedly out of the business?
  • Would you need to engage a recruiter to replace the role externally, or is there a natural successor?
  • What processes, relationships, and knowledge does this person own that aren’t documented anywhere?
  • How and when would you communicate about this person’s absence?
  • Who would need to be informed, and in what order?
  • Do key stakeholders know about this plan, and have you discussed this with them to ensure alignment?
  • What are your wishes in the event you pass away or leave the business? Would you want it to keep going, be sold, or wind down?

This written plan came in handy when a leader left the business months later. Instead of scrambling, I simply referred to the plan and ended up promoting a team member who was identified as a clear successor.

This also helped me imagine my own exit, whether because of an accident or leaving voluntarily. We need to ask ourselves hard questions as founders, one of which is “how would my business carry on without me, and what would my team need to succeed?”

Document key processes, people, and passwords

Knowing who would step in once you’re gone isn’t the same as ensuring everything in your head, and those of your leaders, is documented for that person. When I took parental leave, I created a Notion CEO playbook that outlined all key processes and functions that I owned and that no one else had insight into, including tutorial videos, contact information, written explanations, and links (there’s a full breakdown of prepping for parental leave in this article I wrote for BetaKit). It was a brain dump of everything I owned, and I felt so much peace of mind after I shared it with our COO, who acted as CEO while I was on leave.

You should document:

  • Key logins and passwords (I use 1Password and have a shared vault for many key accounts).
  • Key contacts for lawyers, board members, or other stakeholders that leaders don’t interface with as often.
  • Key accountabilities and priorities, with deadlines and/or cadence if applicable (for example, “send investor update every quarter” with instructions on how to do that).
  • Clear access to key documents and artifacts.

This can feel overwhelming to build, so you can work with an ops team, executive assistant, or virtual assistant to compile everything. And unlike when I created mine in 2021, AI tools can support it as well, if you’re comfortable using them. I asked Claude how it could help me with my succession plan, and it suggested drafting the plan outline, prompting the questions that should be considered, and helping to fill in gaps from scanning my ongoing communications and documents. It then recommended setting up a scheduled task that would audit my email, Slack, and Notion on a regular basis to both identify key stakeholder relationships and how they’ve changed over time, and keep information up to date.

Consider key person insurance

When we raised our first round of institutional funding, one of the stipulations was that we take out a key person life insurance policy and critical illness insurance on me. This means that if I have to step away from the business due to an illness, or if I pass away, the business will receive a payout in order to help with continuity (paying a recruiter, supporting bereavement resources for the team, hiring external resources to support during a transition, or any other costs).

While this is usually required by investors, it’s important to consider for any founder and for any of your key executives. It’s inexpensive and ensures that your business will have the buffer to figure out what’s next.

Ensure your plans are in order

As a founder, your business is one of your key assets, and if you are ill, injured, incapacitated, or pass away, you want to ensure you have proper estate plans in place that allow the people you choose to manage your business.

For example, power of attorney documents name someone to manage your finances if you’re incapacitated, and this person can do anything related to your business that you can do, except for acting as the director of a corporation. This is especially important if you’re a consultant or sole proprietor and you don’t have staff who can step in to support.

When you pass away, a carry-on business clause in your will means the executor can act on your behalf related to the business: keeping it active, winding it down, selling it, or taking other actions. Your will also instructs how your business assets should pass on (unless you have shareholder documents that outline this already), and a dual will can also separate your business assets from your personal assets to reduce probate fees owing.

And, as a business owner, term life insurance can be an inexpensive way to ensure your family would have the funds they need to carry on in your absence.

Keep it current

Your succession plan needs to be reviewed regularly, not just after a key person exits or is promoted. This can be an annual to-do you complete around tax time or in the New Year. Remember, this plan only works if it’s current.

For me, succession planning hits close to home. At Willful, I see daily the impact of people who don’t put plans in place. And as someone who has also been on parental leave twice, I’ve seen firsthand the need to create structures that allow us to step away. As a former business coach said to me, it’s about being needed but not necessary to run your business. Ensure that playbook is in place for your business, so it doesn’t end up in the lurch like Nvidia.
